description: I'm a Computer Engineering student specializing in AI & ML, passionate about space technology, scientific exploration, and innovation. My skills include Python, machine learning, React, TypeScript, FastAPI, and data analysis. I'm participating independently in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under ASTERA, developing an interactive AI-powered space-learning platform.
summary:
ASTERA is a space exploration and learning platform that I developed to tell the stories of human-made equipment left behind during space missions. Inspired by NASA's “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge, the project focuses on preserving the history of these objects and helping people understand why they were sent, what they accomplished, and what remains of them today.

Through ASTERA, users can explore an interactive 3D solar system, discover historic Moon and Mars missions, learn about spacecraft and scientific equipment, and understand what happened to them after their missions ended. I have also incorporated educational content, mission timelines, planetary exploration views, and interactive simulations to make learning more engaging.

I wanted to build ASTERA because space exploration is not just about successful launches or major discoveries. Every mission leaves behind a story, whether it is a rover that completed its journey, equipment that continues to travel through space, or scientific instruments that helped us understand another world. ASTERA brings these stories together in one place and makes them easier for students and space enthusiasts to discover and appreciate.
details:
ASTERA — Every Mission Leaves a Mark

ASTERA is an interactive space exploration and educational platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, inspired by the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.” The project focuses on documenting the stories of human-made spacecraft, landers, rovers, scientific instruments, and other mission equipment that remain on the Moon, Mars, or continue travelling through space.

What does the project do, and how does it work?

ASTERA brings space mission information together in an interactive digital archive. Users can explore a stylized 3D solar system, discover historical space missions, learn about equipment left behind after mission completion, and understand the purpose and contributions of these objects.

The platform includes a searchable mission archive, individual mission information pages, mission timelines, a schematic Moon and Mars exploration atlas, and interactive educational features. It also provides a Space Academy for learning, an educational mission calculator, and a simulated science workbench.

A key aspect of ASTERA is its approach to mission lifecycle classification. Instead of treating every inactive spacecraft as abandoned, the platform distinguishes between equipment remaining on planetary surfaces, spacecraft still travelling through space, decommissioned or inactive hardware, and missions that ended through loss of contact or impact. This helps users understand what actually happened to each mission asset.

What benefits does it offer?

ASTERA makes space exploration history more accessible and engaging. Information about historic missions and their equipment is often spread across different scientific archives and mission websites. ASTERA provides a more approachable way to discover these stories in one place.

Its interactive visualizations and educational activities help students, educators, and space enthusiasts understand complex space missions without needing advanced technical knowledge. It also encourages curiosity about planetary exploration, space science, engineering, and the long-term legacy of human exploration.

What is the intended impact?

The main goal of ASTERA is to preserve the history and significance of human-made objects beyond Earth. Space missions are usually remembered for their launches, discoveries, and achievements, but the equipment that remains after a mission also represents an important part of that history.

Through ASTERA, I want to encourage people to look beyond mission success and understand the scientific, technological, and historical value of these objects. The project aims to make space heritage easier to explore, support space education, and inspire students to learn more about humanity's exploration of the solar system.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

The project was developed using the following technologies:

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D visualization: Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Database: PostgreSQL with pgvector.
  • Additional services: Redis.
  • Mobile development: React Native and Expo.
  • Data and infrastructure: SQLAlchemy, Alembic, and Docker.

For research and mission information, I used NASA and NSSDCA resources, including official mission pages and the supplementary catalogue of human-made material on the Moon. The platform includes a source registry and a NASA page retrieval workflow, with extracted information intended for human review.

How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of ASTERA is the way it transforms space mission records into an exploratory experience. Rather than presenting information only through conventional articles or tables, it allows users to navigate a stylized 3D solar system and discover the stories of mission equipment through interactive visual elements.

I also wanted to make the experience meaningful beyond visual exploration. The mission archive, lifecycle classifications, educational activities, timelines, and simulations connect the historical, scientific, and educational aspects of space exploration.

The central idea behind ASTERA is that a mission does not lose its significance when communication ends or its hardware stops functioning. Every piece of equipment has a story, and those stories deserve to be documented.

What factors were considered during development?

I considered several factors while designing and developing ASTERA:

  1. Scientific accuracy: Mission information should be based on NASA and NSSDCA references. Unverified details should not be presented as established facts.
  2. Correct lifecycle classification: Surface equipment, inactive spacecraft, travelling probes, and crashed or lost hardware should not all be labelled as abandoned.
  3. Accessibility: The platform should make technical space exploration information understandable to students and general audiences.
  4. User experience: Navigation, visualizations, and learning features should make exploration engaging without overwhelming users.
  5. Data transparency: The distinction between sourced mission information, educational simulations, and illustrative visualizations should remain clear.
  6. Scalability: The architecture should support adding more missions, artifacts, scientific references, and educational features over time.
  7. Responsible representation: ASTERA is an independent educational project and does not claim NASA endorsement or represent its visual simulations as official NASA data.

Ultimately, ASTERA was built around one simple idea: Every mission leaves a mark, and every mark has a story worth remembering.
